newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Clarke balances prudence, political expediency.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Clarke balances prudence, political expediency.

text.p: Britain's finance minister Kenneth Clarke tried to balance his reputation as a prudent manager of the economy with the need to win back voters apparently weary of Conservative rule in his last pre-election budget on Tuesday.

But by failing to rein in public borrowing by as much as many City economists believe he should have, he risks having to order politically unpopular interest rate increases before the election, which is due by May 22.

The Chancellor of the Exchequer, who had warned that the electorate would not be swayed by unsustainable tax cuts, opted for only a modest reduction in income tax which was fully offset by indirect tax increases and curbs on public spending.

He painted a rosy picture of Britain's economic outlook, saying growth would accelerate to 3.5 percent in 1997 from 2.5 percent this year and public borrowing would fall enough to ensure Britain met the criteria for joining a single European currency, if it chose to do so.
And despite an unexpected surge in underlying annual inflation to 3.3 percent last month, he insisted he would meet his target of 2.5 percent or less next year.

But City economists, many of whom had argued that Clarke should actually be raising tax to help balance the budget and restrain consumer spending, said there was a risk that he might have to raise interest rates again before the election.
"It is politically astute and in the main, financially sound," said Rob Hayward, an economist at Bank of America.

"The good news is that the budget provides for fiscal tightening, the bad news is that it does not do enough. The budget is unlikely to deter speculation that another rate hike is just a matter of time. It may win a few friends at the polls, but it should also lose some points in the markets."
As widely predicted, the centrepiece of the budget was a reduction in the standard rate of income tax to 23 percent from 24 percent.

Clarke boasted that he could have lopped two percentage points off. "But I preferred instead to raise personal allowances and widen the 20 pence band for those at the bottom end of the the scale," he said.
To offset the cuts in the income tax burden, rises were announced in indirect taxes on items such as cars, petrol and cigarettes and Clarke also promised a crackdown on corporate tax avoidance.

One measure that could antagonise the middle classes was delayed until well after the election -- profit-related pay, under which some employees receive a portion of their pay free of tax if it is linked to company profits, will be reduced from 1998 and scrapped from 2000.
Predictably, Conservative politicians welcomed the budget but privately, some grumbled at the absence of a major tax giveaway.
Opposition Labour party leader Tony Blair, whose party has a strong lead in opinion polls, described it as "the last gasp budget of a government whose time is up."
Business leaders, traditionally firm backers of Conservative policies, appeared lukewarm in their response.

"A penny cut in income tax will do nothing for business and investment," said David Richardson, president of the British Chambers of Commerce. "The worry for business is that, while the cut is affordable to the Exchequer, it may not be affordable to business if interest rates have to rise."

The Confederation of British Industry was pleased that the income tax cut had been limited to what it called an acceptable level but said: "There are concerns about the number of tax changes which will add to business costs."
Philip Shaw, chief economist at Union Discount, said that although fiscal policy appeared to have been tightened, the budget had not changed the outlook for interest rates.

"Bank of England Governor Eddie will still be concerned over the disappointing inflation profile (something not helped by the increases in indirect taxation) and the growing strength of the eocnomy, especially consumer spending," he said.
Clarke unexpectedly raised official interest rates to six percent from 5.75 percent on October 30 to choke off future inflationary pressures.
But he would be reluctant to raise them again in the run-up to the election as this would mean more expensive loans for millions of home-owners.

David Kern, chief economist at National Westminster Bank, said the budget was "ingenious as well as prudent" but predicted that interest rates would still have to rise, possibly to 6.50 percent before the election, which must be held by May 22.
Like many economists, Kern was sceptical of the Chancellor's prediction that the budget defeicit would be cut by four billion pounds ($6.6 billion) to 19 billion in the 1997/98 financial year.

"There will be some natural scepticism as to whether the official public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) forecast indicated in today's budget will prove to be realistic," he said. ($1=.5990 Pound)
